person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: whether advanced mathematical thought rests on the language faculty or on evolutionarily older circuits for number and space
span.quote: The origins of human abilities for mathematics are debated: Some theories suggest that they are founded upon evolutionarily ancient brain circuits for number and space and others that they are grounded in language competence.

span.label: which brain areas professional mathematicians engage when judging advanced mathematical statements, and whether they are language areas or number areas
span.quote: Many mathematicians, however, argue that number concepts are too simple to be representative of advanced mathematics. To address this criticism, here we study the cerebral representation of high-level mathematical concepts in professional mathematicians.

span.label: shows a bilateral parietal, inferior temporal and prefrontal network active for all four branches of mathematics in experts only, sparing language areas and overlapping the circuits for numerals and arithmetic
span.quote: In professional mathematicians only, mathematical statements, whether in algebra, analysis, topology or geometry, activated a reproducible set of bilateral frontal, Intraparietal, and ventrolateral temporal regions. Crucially, these activations spared areas related to language and to general-knowledge semantics.

span.label: existence
span.quote: The evidence suggests that high-level mathematical expertise and basic number sense share common roots in a nonlinguistic brain circuit.

span.label: high-level mathematical reasoning in expert mathematicians
span.quote: To evaluate what brain systems underlie higher mathematics, we scanned professional mathematicians and mathematically naive subjects of equal academic standing as they evaluated the truth of advanced mathematical and nonmathematical statements.

span.label: fmri
span.quote: We collected fMRIs in 15 professional mathematicians and 15 nonmathematician controls of equal academic standing while participants performed fast semantic judgments on mathematical and nonmathematical statements ( Fig. 1 A ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Prolonged exposure to mathematical symbols reshapes ventral visual cortex, amplifying symbol responses and displacing face responses, in the same way reading expertise does for letters
span.quote: mathematical expertise leads to a bilateral enhancement of the visual representation of mathematical symbols.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Because advanced mathematics and basic arithmetic share the same cortical circuit, early number skills and later mathematical achievement are developmentally linked through that shared substrate
span.quote: The fact that these brain areas are jointly involved in higher mathematics and basic arithmetic may explain the bidirectional developmental relationships that have been reported between prelinguistic number skills and later mathematical skills

span.label: expertise amplifies responses at sites that already respond to numerals and formulas in non-experts, rather than recruiting new territory
span.quote: Rather, mathematical judgments were related to an amplification of brain activity at sites that are activated by numbers and formulas in nonmathematicians, with a corresponding reduction in nearby face responses.

span.label: the ventral visual change mirrors literacy, where learning to read shifts responses toward letters and away from faces
span.quote: Those results are analogous to previous findings on literacy, showing that the acquisition of expertise in reading shifts the responses of left ventral visual cortex toward letters and away from faces

span.label: the enhanced formula response reflects a genuine increase in activated cortical volume, not just tighter anatomical alignment in the expert group
span.quote: First, the left inferior temporal activation to written mathematical formulas was significantly enhanced in mathematicians relative to controls (−53 −64 −17, t = 4.27) ( Fig. 8 B ). Single-subject ROI analyses verified that this effect was not simply due to greater variance in anatomical localization in controls compared with mathematicians, but to a genuine increase in the volume of bilateral IT cortex activated by mathematical formulas

span.label: the caudate shifts its engagement to whichever domain the subject is expert in, consistent with a role in motivation and attention
span.quote: First, a group × problem type interaction revealed a striking group difference in the bilateral head of the caudate nucleus ( SI Appendix , Fig. S11 ). This region was active in mathematicians only when they were exposed to math statements and, in control subjects, only when they were exposed to nonmath statements. Thus, the engagement of this subcortical region, which is known to participate in motivation and executive attention, shifted radically toward the subject’s preferred domain.

span.label: language contributes transiently at the angular gyrus during sentence comprehension, and that area is deactivated during the reflection itself
span.quote: However, in mathematicians only, it also showed a greater activation for meaningful than for meaningless math ( SI Appendix , Fig. S12 ). Thus, mathematical expertise enables the left angular gyrus, which is engaged in sentence-level semantic integration ( 35 , 36 ), to extend this function to mathematical statements. Importantly, this contribution is only transient, restricted to the sentence comprehension period, because this area was deactivated during mathematical reflection.

span.label: The group differences in ventral visual responses (formulas, tools, faces) cannot yet be tied to behaviour or shown to be caused by mathematical training.
span.quote: These intriguing differences must be considered with caution because their behavioral impact and causal link to mathematical training remains presently unknown.

span.label: The design cannot rule out a transient role of language areas during the acquisition of mathematical concepts; only learning studies could settle it.
span.quote: Imaging studies of the learning process would be needed to resolve this point.

span.label: Mathematicians and controls may differ on uncontrolled dimensions such as IQ or musical talent, which the authors argue is irrelevant to the within-group dissociation but is not measured.
span.quote: Although mathematicians and controls may still differ on dimensions such as IQ, musical talent, hobbies, etc., such putative differences are irrelevant to our main conclusion of a dissociation between general-knowledge and mathematical reasoning within the mathematicians.

span.label: the authors flag the ventral visual group differences as needing caution, since their behavioural impact and causal link to mathematical training are unknown
span.quote: These intriguing differences must be considered with caution because their behavioral impact and causal link to mathematical training remains presently unknown.

span.label: a small language-area overlap in left BA44 appeared only in smoothed group images and failed to reach significance in single subjects
span.quote: A very small area of overlap could be seen in the left dorsal Brodmann area 44 ( SI Appendix , Fig. S8 B ), an area also singled out in previous reports ( 34 ) and which should certainly be further investigated in future research. Note, however, that this small overlap was present only in smoothed group images and failed to reach significance in higher resolution single-subject results

span.label: controls were near chance on the mathematical statements, so the expertise interaction rests on a group that could not do the task
span.quote: Unsurprisingly, they fell close to chance level with math (37% correct, chance level = 33%; P = 0.014): They managed to perform above chance in detecting which statements were meaningful or meaningless (d′ = 0.67, P = 0.002) but could not identify their truth value (d′ = 0.38, n.s.).

span.label: objective performance was matched but each group rated its own domain as more comfortable
span.quote: Although objective performance on nonmath problems did not differ for mathematicians and controls, their subjective ratings of comprehension, confidence, or difficulty, collected after the fMRI session, revealed that each group felt more comfortable with its respective expertise domain

span.label: the expertise-driven ventral visual shift toward symbols and away from faces, transposed from literacy to mathematics
span.quote: Those results are analogous to previous findings on literacy, showing that the acquisition of expertise in reading shifts the responses of left ventral visual cortex toward letters and away from faces

span.label: representational similarity, used to test whether math, arithmetic and numeral viewing share an activation topography within each subject
span.quote: Second, we used representational similarity analysis to probe whether a similar pattern of activation was evoked, within each subject, by all math-related activities: i.e., mathematical reflection, calculation, and numbers or formula recognition.

span.label: an eighth stimulus category of circular checkerboards, built so that its retinotopic extent EXCEEDED that of every other category
span.quote: plus a control condition consisting of circular checkerboards whose retinotopic extent exceeded that of all other stimuli

span.label: meaningful versus meaningless is the paper's second, ORTHOGONAL criterion - it holds lexical content constant and so tests the same claim without the math-versus-nonmath comparison
span.quote: As a second criterion for brain areas involved in mathematical expertise, we compared the activations during reflection on meaningful versus meaningless mathematical statements. This contrast, which is orthogonal to the previous one and controls for lexical content, fully replicated the above results.

span.label: difficulty here has an objective form (percent correct, matched) and a subjective form (rated, slightly higher for math), and the paper's controls address the second
span.quote: However, subjective difficulty, as reported by mathematicians after the fMRI, was judged as slightly higher for the math problems than for the nonmath problems (on a subjective scale converted to a 0–100 score: subjective difficulty = 52.4 ± 3.4 for math, and 40.0 ± 4.5 for nonmath; t = 2.4, P = 0.03).

span.label: the visual number form area is defined by responding to Arabic numerals more than letters or pictures, and was previously hard to detect because it sits near a zone of fMRI signal loss
span.quote: The VNFAs were previously difficult to detect with fMRI because they lie close to a zone of fMRI signal loss ( 18 ). However, using a fast high-resolution fMRI sequence that mitigates these difficulties, we found that the VNFAs are easily detectable and are activated bilaterally not only by Arabic numerals, but also by algebraic formulas, arithmetic problems, and, in mathematicians only, during high-level mathematical reasoning.

span.label: the multiple demand system is the rival account: a set of areas active in any hard task, which overlaps the math network and is why difficulty had to be excluded
span.quote: The activations observed during mathematical reflection overlap with a set of areas that have been termed the “multiple demand system” ( 29 ). Those regions are active during a variety of cognitive tasks that involve executive control and task difficulty ( 30 ). It is therefore important to evaluate whether our results can be imputed to a greater task difficulty for math relative to nonmath statements.

span.label: language areas here are defined by an independent localiser in the same subjects, not by anatomy, so the sparing claim is about functionally identified voxels
span.quote: To further probe the contribution of language areas to math, we used a sensitive region-of-interest (ROI) analysis. We selected left-hemispheric regions previously reported ( 32 ) as showing a language-related activation proportional to constituent size during sentence processing [temporal pole (TP); anterior superior temporal sulcus (aSTS); posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS); temporo-parietal junction (TPj); inferior frontal gyrus pars orbitalis (IFGorb), and pars triangularis (IFGtri)], plus the left Brodmann area 44 ( 33 ). We then used an independent functional localizer ( 28 ) to identify subject-specific peaks of activation to sentences (spoken or written) relative to rest and finally tested the contribution of those language voxels to the main reasoning task.

span.label: replicates → earlier observations of number-sense and number-form areas (cited as references 16, 18, 37)
span.quote: Both calculation and simple number processing activated bilateral IPS and IT, thus replicating early observations of number-sense and number-form areas ( Fig. 6 ).

span.label: contradicts → the hypothesis that mathematics is an offshoot of language syntax, attributed in the article to Noam Chomsky (reference 1)
span.quote: Together, those results are inconsistent with the hypothesis that language syntax plays a specific role in the algebraic abilities of expert adults.

span.label: contradicts → the hypothesis that mathematical capacity is an abstraction from linguistic operations
span.quote: According to one hypothesis, mathematics, like other cultural abilities that appeared suddenly with modern humans in the upper Paleolithic, is an offshoot of the human language faculty—for Noam Chomsky, for instance, “the origin of the mathematical capacity [lies in] an abstraction from linguistic operations” ( 1 ). Many mathematicians and physicists, however, disagree and insist that mathematical reflection is primarily nonlinguistic—Albert Einstein, for instance, stated: “Words and language, whether written or spoken, do not seem to play any part in my thought processes.

span.label: supports → the account grounding mathematics in ancient nonlinguistic intuitions of number and space
span.quote: The evidence suggests that high-level mathematical expertise and basic number sense share common roots in a nonlinguistic brain circuit.

span.label: extends → arithmetic imaging work, by answering the objection that number concepts are too simple to represent advanced mathematics
span.quote: Many mathematicians, however, argue that number concepts are too simple to be representative of advanced mathematics. To address this criticism, here we study the cerebral representation of high-level mathematical concepts in professional mathematicians.

span.quote: However, in mathematicians only, it also showed a greater activation for meaningful than for meaningless math ( SI Appendix , Fig. S12 ). Thus, mathematical expertise enables the left angular gyrus, which is engaged in sentence-level semantic integration ( 35 , 36 ), to extend this function to mathematical statements. Importantly, this contribution is only transient, restricted to the sentence comprehension period, because this area was deactivated during mathematical reflection.

Although there was no significant difference between the two groups at the principal peak of the right FFA, a whole-brain search indicated that responses to faces were significantly reduced in mathematicians relative to controls in right-hemispheric IT (44 −45 −17, t = 4.72)

Remarkably, those activations overlapped entirely with the regions activated by higher level mathematics in mathematicians only

span.quote: Second, we used representational similarity analysis to probe whether a similar pattern of activation was evoked, within each subject, by all math-related activities: i.e., mathematical reflection, calculation, and numbers or formula recognition.

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: entered into a second-level whole-brain ANOVA with stimulus category as within-subject factor

span.label: F-test
span.quote: Differences in cortical responses across mathematical domains were evaluated by an F-test at the whole-brain level (voxel P < 0.001, cluster P < 0.05 corrected).

span.quote: Mean d′ values for discrimination of meaningful versus meaningless statements

span.label: correction for multiple comparisons
span.quote: All brain-activation results are reported with a clusterwise threshold of P < 0.05 corrected for multiple comparisons across the whole brain, using an uncorrected voxelwise threshold of P < 0.001.

span.label: correlation
span.quote: For each subject, we first computed the matrix of correlations between the activations evoked by each of the experimental conditions

span.label: Student t tests
span.quote: However, subjective difficulty, as reported by mathematicians after the fMRI, was judged as slightly higher for the math problems than for the nonmath problems (on a subjective scale converted to a 0–100 score: subjective difficulty = 52.4 ± 3.4 for math, and 40.0 ± 4.5 for nonmath; t = 2.4, P = 0.03).

span.label: cluster P < 0.05 corrected
span.quote: Second, to directly evaluate the impact of difficulty on the observed brain networks, within each subject, we sorted the meaningful math and nonmath statements into two levels of subjective difficulty (easy or difficult: i.e., below or above the subject’s mean of the corresponding category). As expected, the easiest math statements were rated as much easier than the difficult nonmath statements ( Fig. 5 A ). Despite this difference, the contrast of meaningful easy math > meaningful difficult nonmath again revealed the same sites as the ones that were activated for the standard math > nonmath contrast ( Fig. 5 B ). Thus, those sites were activated even during simple mathematical reflection, and their greater activation for math than for nonmath occurred irrespective of task difficulty.

span.label: In professional mathematicians, reflection on advanced mathematics activated a bilateral fronto-parietal and inferior temporal network that did not include classical language or general-semantic areas.
span.quote: Crucially, these activations spared areas related to language and to general-knowledge semantics.

span.label: The same math network was engaged by all four tested branches of mathematics and even transiently by meaningless mathematical statements.
span.quote: It was activated by all domains of mathematics tested (analysis, algebra, topology, and geometry) and even, transiently, by meaningless mathematical statements.

span.label: Non-mathematical general-knowledge reflection recruited a separate anterior temporal and angular gyrus semantic network.
span.quote: Instead, such problems activated distinct bilateral anterior temporal and angular regions.

span.label: A region-of-interest analysis of language areas showed mathematics engaged them no more, and often less, than general semantic reasoning did.
span.quote: Thus, if anything, mathematics called less upon those language regions than did general semantic reasoning.

span.label: The high-level mathematics network overlapped the parietal and inferior temporal sites activated by simple calculation and by the mere sight of numerals, and this overlap survived removal of statements containing any numerical reference.
span.quote: Thus, the overlapping activations to number and to advanced math cannot be explained by a shared component of numerical knowledge but indicate that high-level mathematics recruits the same brain circuit as basic arithmetic.

span.label: The math-versus-nonmath activation difference could not be attributed to task difficulty, since even the easiest math problems activated the network more than the hardest nonmath problems.
span.quote: Thus, those sites were activated even during simple mathematical reflection, and their greater activation for math than for nonmath occurred irrespective of task difficulty.

span.label: Mathematical expertise was accompanied by expanded number and formula responses in the left visual number form area.
span.quote: Thus, mathematical expertise is associated with a small expansion of number representations in the left VNFA and a bilateral recruitment of the VNFA by mathematical formulas.

span.label: mathematicians performed equally on math and non-math statements, 63% against 65% correct
span.quote: Math and nonmath problems were well-matched in objective difficulty level because mathematicians performed identically on both (63% and 65% correct) ( Fig. 1 B and SI Appendix , Supplementary Results ).

span.label: controls matched mathematicians on non-math but were near chance on math
span.quote: Unsurprisingly, they fell close to chance level with math (37% correct, chance level = 33%; P = 0.014): They managed to perform above chance in detecting which statements were meaningful or meaningless (d′ = 0.67, P = 0.002) but could not identify their truth value (d′ = 0.38, n.s.).

span.label: all four branches of mathematics activated the same bilateral parietal, temporal and prefrontal network
span.quote: All four domains of mathematics activated those regions, as revealed by a significant intersection of activations to each domain ( Fig. 3 A ) (each at P < 0.001).

span.label: the network stayed active for about fifteen seconds after a math statement and deactivated for non-math
span.quote: Examination of the time course of activity indicated that, at all sites of the shared math network, the fMRI signal rose sharply after a mathematical statement and remained sustained for ∼15 s ( Fig. 2 C and SI Appendix , Fig. S1 ). Contrariwise, for nonmathematical statements, a slow deactivation was seen

span.label: in controls the math contrast landed on the sites for meaningless statements
span.quote: In control subjects, the math > nonmath contrast yielded a different set of regions that overlapped with the sites activated by meaningless nonmath statements ( SI Appendix , Fig. S2 and Table S1 ), suggesting that math statements sounded like gibberish to nonmathematicians.

span.label: essentially no intersection between the math and general-knowledge semantic networks, and none in perisylvian language cortex even at a lenient threshold
span.quote: Crucially, there was essentially no intersection at P < 0.001 of the areas for meaningful > meaningless math and for meaningful > meaningless nonmath ( Fig. 4 A and SI Appendix , Tables S1 and S3 ). The only small area of intersection, suggesting a role in generic reflection and decision making, was observed outside the classical language network, in bilateral superior frontal (BA 8) and left inferior MFG. Even at a lower threshold ( P < 0.01 uncorrected), the intersection extended to part of posterior parietal and dorsal PFC but spared perisylvian language cortex.

span.label: language regions defined by an independent localiser were engaged no more by math than by general reasoning, and often less
span.quote: All regions were activated during sentence presentation ( SI Appendix , Fig. S7 ), either identically across conditions, or more for nonmath than for math and/or for controls than for mathematicians ( SI Appendix , Table S5 ). Thus, if anything, mathematics called less upon those language regions than did general semantic reasoning.

span.label: the math network overlapped the areas for arithmetic and for merely viewing numerals
span.quote: Both calculation and simple number processing activated bilateral IPS and IT, thus replicating early observations of number-sense and number-form areas ( Fig. 6 ). Remarkably, those activations overlapped entirely with the regions activated by higher level mathematics in mathematicians only

span.label: CONFOUND REVERSED: easy math contrasted against difficult non-math still produced the same sites
span.quote: Second, to directly evaluate the impact of difficulty on the observed brain networks, within each subject, we sorted the meaningful math and nonmath statements into two levels of subjective difficulty (easy or difficult: i.e., below or above the subject’s mean of the corresponding category). As expected, the easiest math statements were rated as much easier than the difficult nonmath statements ( Fig. 5 A ). span.label: CONTROL NULL: contrasting difficult against easy statements within each domain revealed no significant sites at all
span.quote: This result was confirmed by the contrast of difficult > easy math and difficult > easy nonmath, which revealed no significant sites.

span.label: ORTHOGONAL REPLICATION: the meaningful-versus-meaningless math contrast, which holds words constant, reproduced the whole result
span.quote: As a second criterion for brain areas involved in mathematical expertise, we compared the activations during reflection on meaningful versus meaningless mathematical statements. This contrast, which is orthogonal to the previous one and controls for lexical content, fully replicated the above results.

span.label: CONTENT REANALYSIS: excluding statements with any indirect numerical reference left the activation virtually unchanged
span.quote: Our mathematical statements carefully avoided any direct mention of numbers or arithmetic facts ( SI Appendix ), but some still contained an occasional indirect reference to numbers or to fractions (e.g., ℝ 2 , unit sphere, semi-major axis, etc). We therefore reanalyzed the results after systematic exclusion of such statements. The activation evoked by mathematical reflection remained virtually unchanged ( SI Appendix , Fig. S9 and Table S6 ). Thus, the overlapping activations to number and to advanced math cannot be explained by a shared component of numerical knowledge but indicate that high-level mathematics recruits the same brain circuit as basic arithmetic.

span.label: HAZARD NAMED ABOUT THEIR OWN RESULT: group-level overlap can arise from intersubject averaging, so the overlap was retested within subjects
span.quote: Because group-level overlap of activation can arise artificially from intersubject averaging, we next turned to more sensitive within-subject analyses.

span.label: the within-subject pattern analyses confirmed that advanced math, arithmetic and numeral viewing share cortical sites in trained individuals
span.quote: Overall, these high-resolution single-subject analyses confirm that advanced mathematics, basic arithmetic, and even the mere viewing of numbers and formulas recruit similar and overlapping cortical sites in mathematically trained individuals.

span.label: 72 and 18 — number of mathematical statements (18 per domain) and of nonmathematical statements presented in the auditory runs
span.quote: Subjects were presented with 72 mathematical statements (18 in each of the fields of analysis, algebra, topology, and geometry) and 18 nonmathematical statements.

span.label: 15 and 15 — professional mathematicians and non-mathematician controls of equal academic standing
span.quote: We collected fMRIs in 15 professional mathematicians and 15 nonmathematician controls of equal academic standing while participants performed fast semantic judgments on mathematical and nonmathematical statements ( Fig. 1 A ). On each trial, a short spoken sentence was followed by a 4-s reflection period during which the participants decided whether the statement was true, false, or meaningless. Meaningful and meaningless statements were matched on duration and lexical content, but meaningless statements could be quickly dismissed, whereas meaningful statements required in-depth thinking, thus presumably activating brain areas involved in conceptual knowledge.

span.label: 63% and 65% — mathematicians' accuracy on math and non-math, the basis for calling the two matched in difficulty
span.quote: Math and nonmath problems were well-matched in objective difficulty level because mathematicians performed identically on both (63% and 65% correct) ( Fig. 1 B and SI Appendix , Supplementary Results ).

span.label: 37% against 33% chance — controls' accuracy on mathematical statements
span.quote: Unsurprisingly, they fell close to chance level with math (37% correct, chance level = 33%; P = 0.014): They managed to perform above chance in detecting which statements were meaningful or meaningless (d′ = 0.67, P = 0.002) but could not identify their truth value (d′ = 0.38, n.s.).

span.label: 52.4 against 40.0 — subjective difficulty for math and non-math on a 0-100 scale, the only difficulty difference found
span.quote: However, subjective difficulty, as reported by mathematicians after the fMRI, was judged as slightly higher for the math problems than for the nonmath problems (on a subjective scale converted to a 0–100 score: subjective difficulty = 52.4 ± 3.4 for math, and 40.0 ± 4.5 for nonmath; t = 2.4, P = 0.03).

span.label: about 15 s — how long the math network stayed active after a statement
span.quote: Examination of the time course of activity indicated that, at all sites of the shared math network, the fMRI signal rose sharply after a mathematical statement and remained sustained for ∼15 s ( Fig. 2 C and SI Appendix , Fig. S1 ).
